title: Flexbox in depth: navbars and card rows
goal: Use Flexbox to build a real navbar and a row of cards that line up and wrap properly.

concepts: Flex container vs flex items: display:flex goes on the parent
Main axis and cross axis; flex-direction row vs column
justify-content (main axis) and align-items (cross axis)
gap instead of margins between items
flex-wrap, and flex: 1 / flex-grow / flex-shrink / flex-basis
margin-left: auto to push an item to the far end

build.task: In day07/, build a page with (1) a navbar: logo text on the left, 4 links on the right, all vertically centred; (2) a row of 4 cards (title, short text, button) that sit side by side with equal widths on a wide screen and wrap onto new lines when the window is narrow; (3) a footer with three columns of links. Use Flexbox only, no Grid and no floats.

acceptance: Logo left and links right in the navbar, vertically centred, using justify-content or margin-left:auto
Spacing between items uses gap, not margins on every item
Cards have equal widths on a wide window and wrap on a narrow one (flex-wrap plus flex-basis or flex: 1 1 200px)
All card buttons line up at the bottom even when card text lengths differ
Footer has three columns side by side
No Grid, no floats, no position:absolute for layout

hints: Build one thing at a time: navbar first, check it, then cards, then footer. Turn on DevTools' flex overlay (the 'flex' badge in the Elements panel) to see the axes.
For wrapping equal cards try .cards { display:flex; flex-wrap:wrap; gap:16px } and .card { flex: 1 1 220px }. The 220px is the width a card wants before it wraps.
To push buttons to the bottom, make each card a column flex container (flex-direction:column) and give the button margin-top:auto.
proof: Commit with day07/index.html and day07/style.css. Include a screenshot of the wide and narrow layouts in day07/screens/ if you can.

explainBack.q: In your navbar, which property puts the links on the right? Explain what it does in terms of the main axis.
lookFor: names their actual property (justify-content: space-between or margin-left:auto)
main axis is horizontal for row
free space is distributed / pushed

explainBack.q: Your cards use a flex value. Read it out and explain each of its three parts.
lookFor: flex-grow: can grow into extra space
flex-shrink: can shrink
flex-basis: starting size before growing/shrinking
wrapping happens when basis no longer fits

explainBack.q: How did you line up the buttons at the bottom of cards with different text lengths?
lookFor: card is a column flex container
margin-top:auto takes the leftover space
cards in a row stretch to same height by default (align-items: stretch)

lastHintExplanation: display:flex lays children along the main axis (horizontal for row). justify-content distributes space on the main axis, align-items aligns on the cross axis. flex: 1 1 220px means grow:1, shrink:1, basis:220px, so cards start at 220px, share extra space, and wrap when fewer fit. Inside a column-flex card, margin-top:auto eats the leftover space and pushes the button down.

predict.q: A div has display:flex and three child divs. With no other CSS, how are the children laid out?
options: Side by side in a row
In a 3-column grid with equal widths
predict.why: The default flex-direction is row, so items sit side by side at their content width.

predict.q: A flex row has 3 items and justify-content: space-between. Where does the middle item sit?
options: Exactly in the centre of the free space between first and last
It wraps to a new line
predict.why: space-between puts the first item at the start, the last at the end, and splits remaining space evenly between items.

title: CSS Grid: two-dimensional page layouts
goal: Lay out a full page (header, sidebar, content, footer) and a photo gallery with CSS Grid.

concepts: display:grid, grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows
The fr unit and repeat()
gap for rows and columns
Placing items with grid-column / grid-row (span)
grid-template-areas for readable page layouts
repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr)) for responsive galleries
When to use Grid (2D) vs Flexbox (1D)

resources.title: CSS-Tricks: A Complete Guide to CSS Grid

build.task: In day08/, build a dashboard-style page using grid-template-areas: header across the top, sidebar on the left, main content, footer across the bottom. Inside main, add a gallery of at least 8 items (images or coloured boxes with captions) using repeat(auto-fit, minmax(...)) so the number of columns changes with the window width. Make one gallery item span 2 columns.

starterFiles.name: day08/index.html
starterFiles.content:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Day 8: Grid</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
</head>
<body class="page">
  <header class="page-header"></header>
  <aside class="page-sidebar"></aside>
  <main class="page-main"></main>
  <footer class="page-footer"></footer>
</body>
</html>

acceptance: The page layout uses grid-template-areas with named areas
The page fills at least the full window height (min-height: 100vh) with the footer at the bottom
The gallery uses repeat(auto-fit or auto-fill, minmax(...)) and changes column count when resizing
At least one gallery item spans 2 columns with grid-column: span 2
gap is used for spacing, not margins

hints: Write the areas like a picture: grid-template-areas: "header header" "sidebar main" "footer footer"; then give each element grid-area: header etc.
For the rows try grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto with min-height:100vh on the body: the middle row takes all the leftover height.
Gallery: .gallery { display:grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(180px, 1fr)); gap:12px }. Open DevTools' grid overlay to see the lines.

explainBack.q: Read your grid-template-areas aloud and explain how the browser turns it into a layout.
lookFor: each string is a row
each word is a column cell
repeated names make an area span
elements placed with grid-area

explainBack.q: Explain what repeat(auto-fit, minmax(180px, 1fr)) does when you make the window narrower.
lookFor: fits as many columns of at least 180px as possible
1fr shares leftover space
columns drop as width shrinks, items move to new rows
no media query needed

explainBack.q: Why did you pick Grid for the page and not Flexbox?
lookFor: grid controls rows and columns together (2D)
flexbox is one direction (1D)
areas make the layout readable

lastHintExplanation: grid-template-areas draws the layout as text: each quoted string is a row, each word a cell, and repeating a name makes that area span. auto-fit with minmax(180px, 1fr) creates as many columns as fit at 180px minimum, then stretches them with 1fr, so the gallery adapts without media queries. Grid is for two-dimensional layouts; Flexbox is for one row or column.

predict.q: A 600px-wide grid has grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr and no gap. How wide are the columns?
A grid has grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr) and 7 children. How many rows are created?
predict.why: Items fill 3 per row: 3 + 3 + 1, so 3 rows; rows are created automatically.

title: Responsive design: mobile-first media queries
goal: Make one page look right on a phone, a tablet and a laptop using mobile-first media queries.

concepts: Why the viewport meta tag is required on phones
Mobile-first: base styles for small screens, then min-width media queries
Media query syntax: @media (min-width: 768px) { ... }
Common breakpoints and why you choose them by content, not devices
DevTools device toolbar for testing widths
Hiding/showing and re-arranging content at breakpoints

build.task: In day09/, build a product page (any product you like): header with nav, hero section (heading, text, image), a features section with 6 features, and a pricing section with 3 plans. Write mobile-first CSS: single column on phones; features in 2 columns from 600px; features in 3 columns and hero text beside the image from 900px. On phones the nav links stack under the logo.
acceptance: Viewport meta tag is present
Base CSS (outside any media query) is the phone layout
Only min-width media queries are used, at least two breakpoints
Features: 1 column on phones, 2 from 600px, 3 from 900px
Hero image and text side by side from 900px, stacked below that
No horizontal scrollbar at 360px width (check in DevTools device toolbar)

hints: Start with the DevTools device toolbar at 360px wide and build the phone version completely before writing any media query.
Then add @media (min-width: 600px) { .features { grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr) } } and check at 600px, then add the 900px block.
If a horizontal scrollbar appears, look for fixed widths (width: 500px) and images without max-width:100%. In DevTools, hover elements to find the one wider than the screen.
proof: Commit with day09/ files, and screenshots at 360px, 768px and 1200px in day09/screens/.

explainBack.q: What does mobile-first mean in your CSS file? Point to the lines that prove it.
lookFor: base styles are for phones
media queries use min-width and add changes for bigger screens
refers to their actual breakpoints

explainBack.q: What happens on a real phone if you delete the viewport meta tag?
lookFor: phone pretends to be ~980px wide
page shown zoomed out and tiny
media queries for small widths don't apply

explainBack.q: How did you choose your breakpoints?
lookFor: where the content starts to look cramped or stretched
not tied to a specific device
tested by resizing

lastHintExplanation: Without the viewport meta tag, phones render the page at a fake desktop width and zoom out. Mobile-first means the CSS outside media queries is the phone layout, and each @media (min-width: X) block adds changes once the screen is at least X wide. Breakpoints should be where your content starts to break, not specific device sizes.

predict.q: CSS: p { color: black } @media (min-width: 768px) { p { color: blue } }. The window is 500px wide. What colour is the text?
predict.why: 500px is less than 768px, so the media query doesn't apply.

predict.q: CSS order: @media (min-width: 600px) { h1 { color: red } } then @media (min-width: 900px) { h1 { color: blue } }. At 1000px, what colour is h1?
predict.why: Both queries match; same specificity, so the later rule wins.

title: CSS units, responsive images and fluid type
goal: Choose the right CSS unit for each job and make images and text scale smoothly on any screen.

concepts: Absolute vs relative units: px, %, em, rem, vw, vh
Why rem is the default choice for font sizes and spacing
max-width: 100% and height: auto for images
object-fit: cover for cropped thumbnails
<picture> and srcset for different image sizes
clamp() for fluid font sizes
min(), max() and max-width containers for readable line length

build.task: In day10/, build a blog article page: a full-width cover image, a title, author line and 5+ paragraphs, plus a grid of 6 square thumbnails. Use rem for all font sizes and spacing, clamp() for the h1 size, a max-width container (about 65ch) for the text, object-fit: cover for the square thumbnails, and srcset on the cover image with at least two sizes.
acceptance: No px font sizes; font sizes and spacing use rem
h1 uses clamp() and grows smoothly as the window widens
Article text column is limited (e.g. max-width: 65ch) and centred
All images have max-width:100% and never overflow
Thumbnails are perfect squares using aspect-ratio: 1 and object-fit: cover without stretching
Cover image uses srcset (and sizes) with at least two image files

hints: Put img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; display: block } at the top of your CSS. Most image overflow problems go away.
Fluid heading: h1 { font-size: clamp(1.75rem, 4vw + 1rem, 3.5rem) } means: never below 1.75rem, never above 3.5rem, and scales with the window in between.
For squares: .thumb { aspect-ratio: 1; width: 100%; object-fit: cover }. To make two image sizes, resize one photo in any image editor (e.g. 800px and 1600px wide).
proof: Commit with day10/ files including your images.

explainBack.q: Explain rem and em using your own CSS. Why did you use rem for font sizes?
lookFor: rem relative to root (html) font size
em relative to the element's/parent's font size
rem doesn't compound when nested
respects the user's browser font setting

explainBack.q: Read your clamp() for the h1 and explain each of the three values.
lookFor: minimum
preferred value that scales with vw
maximum
result stays between min and max

explainBack.q: What does object-fit: cover do to a portrait photo in your square thumbnail?
lookFor: fills the box
keeps aspect ratio, no stretching
crops the overflow

lastHintExplanation: rem is relative to the root font size (usually 16px), so 1.5rem is always 24px no matter where it's nested, and it scales if the user changes their browser font size. em is relative to the current element's font size and compounds when nested. clamp(min, preferred, max) picks the preferred value but keeps it between min and max. object-fit: cover fills the box while keeping proportions, cropping what doesn't fit.

predict.q: The html font size is 16px. A div's parent has font-size: 20px. The div has font-size: 2rem. What is its font size?
predict.why: rem uses the root font size: 2 × 16 = 32px. The parent doesn't matter.

predict.q: A parent has font-size: 20px. Its child has font-size: 1.5em. What is the child's font size?
predict.why: em for font-size is relative to the parent: 1.5 × 20 = 30px.

## Breakpoints

acceptance: plan.md is filled in and committed before the HTML/CSS (check commit order)
All 7 sections exist with semantic elements
Header stays at the top while scrolling (position: sticky)
Course cards: 1 column on phones, 2 on tablets, 3 on desktop
Form fields all have labels; the select lists real course options
No horizontal scroll at 360px; looks intentional at 1440px
Colours and spacing defined once as CSS custom properties (--brand, --space-2 ...)

hints: Commit plan.md first. Then build section by section and commit after each one. Small commits make the history easy to read and errors easy to undo.
position: sticky; top: 0 on the header only works if no ancestor has overflow: hidden. Give the header a background colour so content doesn't show through.
Define :root { --brand: #2563eb; --space-1: 0.5rem; --space-2: 1rem; --space-3: 2rem } and use var(--brand) everywhere. Changing the brand colour then takes one edit.
proof: Link to your repo folder day11/ on GitHub. At least 5 commits for this day.

explainBack.q: Walk through your plan.md. For one section you chose Grid and one you chose Flexbox: why?
lookFor: grid for 2D card grids
flex for a single row/column like nav or hero
decision tied to their actual sections

explainBack.q: How does position: sticky on your header differ from position: fixed?
lookFor: sticky stays in normal flow until it reaches the top offset
fixed is removed from flow and always relative to the viewport
fixed often needs padding on the body to avoid covering content

explainBack.q: What are CSS custom properties and how did they help in this project?
lookFor: variables defined with --name
used with var()
change once, updates everywhere
consistent colours and spacing

lastHintExplanation: Grid suits sections where items line up in rows and columns (course cards); Flexbox suits a single line (nav, a hero with two halves). position: sticky keeps the element in normal flow until scrolling reaches its top offset, then it sticks; fixed removes it from flow entirely. Custom properties (--brand) are variables, so one change updates every use.

predict.q: :root { --gap: 1rem } .grid { gap: var(--gap, 2rem) }. What gap does .grid get?
predict.why: --gap is defined, so var() uses it. The fallback 2rem is used only when the variable is not defined.
